title: Why does partitioning NOT automatically make queries faster — how does the query need to filter on the PARTITION KEY for the database to do partition pruning (skip irrelevant partitions), so a table partitioned by date but queried mostly by `user_id` still scans many partitions — and how do you choose range vs list vs hash partitioning from the actual access pattern?
shortTitle: Why partitioning does not automatically make queries faster — partition pruning and choosing a scheme

s1_definition.profdef: Partitioning speeds up queries only when the database can perform partition pruning — eliminating partitions that cannot satisfy the query — which requires the query to filter on the partition key. A table partitioned by date but queried by a non-key column like `user_id` cannot be pruned, so the engine scans every partition, often performing worse than an unpartitioned table with a good index. The correct partition scheme (range, list, or hash) is therefore dictated by the dominant query's filter column and value distribution, not chosen arbitrarily.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank split its transaction ledger into one book per month (partitioned by date). If a teller asks "show me February's transactions," he grabs only the February book — fast. But if he asks "show me all of Rajesh's transactions," and the books are organized by month not by customer, he must open every monthly book and search each one. Partitioning by the wrong thing for your questions makes you search everything anyway. You organize the books by whatever you most often ask about.
s1_definition.oneliner: Partitioning helps only when the query filters on the partition key so the engine can prune; choose range, list, or hash to match how you actually query.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Partitioning speeds up queries only when the database can perform partition pruning — eliminating partitions that cannot satisfy the query — which requires the query to filter on the partition key. A table partitioned by date but queried by a non-key column like `user_id` cannot be pruned, so the engine scans every partition, often performing worse than an unpartitioned table with a good index. The correct partition scheme (range, list, or hash) is therefore dictated by the dominant query's filter column and value distribution, not chosen arbitrarily.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank split its transaction ledger into one book per month (partitioned by date). If a teller asks "show me February's transactions," he grabs only the February book — fast. But if he asks "show me all of Rajesh's transactions," and the books are organized by month not by customer, he must open every monthly book and search each one. Partitioning by the wrong thing for your questions makes you search everything anyway. You organize the books by whatever you most often ask about.

**One line to remember:** Partitioning helps only when the query filters on the partition key so the engine can prune; choose range, list, or hash to match how you actually query.

sections.s2_technical:
A common misconception is that partitioning is a performance feature you turn on and queries get faster. It is not. Partitioning is primarily a manageability feature, and it improves query speed only through partition pruning, which has a strict precondition: the query must filter on the partition key.

Partition pruning is the planner's ability to look at a query's WHERE clause and eliminate partitions that cannot possibly contain matching rows. If a table is partitioned by `txn_date` into monthly partitions and you run `WHERE txn_date >= '2024-02-01' AND txn_date < '2024-03-01'`, the planner proves that only the February partition can match and scans just that one, skipping all the others. That is where the speedup comes from — reading one small partition instead of the whole table.

Now consider the trap. Suppose the table is partitioned by `txn_date` but your dominant query is `WHERE user_id = 'SAV2001'` with no date filter. The planner has no way to know which months contain Rajesh's transactions, so it cannot prune anything. It must scan every single partition looking for `user_id = 'SAV2001'`. This is often slower than an unpartitioned table, because instead of one index lookup you now do a lookup in every partition, plus the overhead of combining results. The partitioning actively hurt you. The row count did not change; you just scattered the data in a way that does not match how you query it.

This is why the partition key and scheme must be derived from the actual access pattern. You look at your dominant queries and their filter columns and value distributions, then choose:

Range partitioning fits a continuous, ordered key where queries filter by ranges — time above all. Transactions, logs, events queried by date windows are the classic fit, and it also enables cheap archival by dropping old partitions. You choose range when your hot queries say "between this date and that date."

List partitioning fits a discrete key with a small set of known values where queries filter by those values — region, account type, currency, country. You choose list when queries say "where region = SOUTH" and the distinct values are few and stable.

Hash partitioning fits when there is no natural range or list but you need to spread data and load evenly to avoid hot spots, and your queries filter by equality on the key. Hashing `account_id` distributes accounts uniformly across partitions, and a query for one account prunes to the single partition its hash lands in. You choose hash when the key is high-cardinality, there is no useful ordering, and you mainly do equality lookups.

A crucial design move when you query by two dimensions, such as both date ranges and by account, is composite or sub-partitioning: partition by range on date and then sub-partition by hash on account, or include both in the design so both common filters can prune. And the overriding rule is: never partition for its own sake. If your queries do not filter on the partition key, a plain indexed table is usually better, and partitioning should be justified by either pruning that matches your real queries or by manageability needs like archival and maintenance of enormous tables.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India partitioned transactions by month because the table was huge, but the busiest query is "all of a customer's transactions" with no date filter. This is exactly the pruning trap — the planner scans every monthly partition.

Problem 2 — The team wonders why performance got worse after partitioning. This is exactly the point that partitioning does not automatically speed queries — it helps only when the filter matches the partition key.

Problem 3 — We must pick the right scheme. Customer-centric equality queries suggest hashing by account; date-window reporting suggests range by date; region reports suggest list by region. This is exactly how the access pattern dictates range versus list versus hash.

We will build a `PartitionChoiceService` that, given the dominant query's filter column and distribution, recommends range, list, or hash, and show a composite range-plus-hash design so both date-window and per-account queries can prune.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__composite_partition.sql
-- WRONG for a user-centric workload: partitioned by date but queried by account_id.
--   SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001';  -- scans EVERY month (no pruning)

-- COMPOSITE: range by date (for reports) THEN hash by account (for per-customer lookups),
-- so BOTH common filters can prune.
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGSERIAL,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    txn_date   DATE NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (txn_id, txn_date, account_id)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (txn_date);

CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_02 PARTITION OF transactions
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01')
    PARTITION BY HASH (account_id);          -- sub-partition by account

CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_02_h0 PARTITION OF transactions_2024_02
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_02_h1 PARTITION OF transactions_2024_02
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
-- ... h2, h3

-- Now: WHERE txn_date in Feb AND account_id='SAV2001'
--   → prunes to Feb, then to the ONE hash partition for SAV2001.
```


sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/partition-strategy-1.0.0.jar

# Prove pruning: filter on the partition key → scans ONE partition
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions \
  WHERE txn_date >= '2024-02-01' AND txn_date < '2024-03-01' AND account_id='SAV2001';"

# Prove the trap: filter only on a NON-key column → scans ALL partitions
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001';"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an access pattern where the dominant query filters by `account_id` and also sometimes by a date window.

Step 1: The access pattern is fed to `PartitionChoiceService`. It is high-cardinality equality on account plus date-window filtering — two dimensions.

Step 2: The service recommends a composite scheme: range by date, sub-partitioned by hash of account. This is chosen precisely because both of our common filters can then prune.

Step 3: With the composite table in place, a query `WHERE txn_date in February AND account_id = 'SAV2001'` first prunes to the February partition, then prunes to the single hash sub-partition that holds SAV2001. The engine scans one small sub-partition.

Step 4: Contrast the trap. If we had only range-by-date and ran `WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'` with no date filter, the planner could not prune at all and would scan every monthly partition, which is slower than a plain indexed table. The data distribution did not change; it was scattered in a way that did not match the query.

Step 5: Had the dominant filter instead been region with a few values, the service would recommend list; had it been pure per-account equality with no date, it would recommend hash; and if no query filtered on any good key, it would recommend not partitioning and using a plain index.

```
2026-10-25 13:52:20 INFO  PartitionChoiceService - Per-account lookups + date windows → COMPOSITE range(date)+hash(account)
2026-10-25 13:52:21 WARN  PartitionChoiceService - No filter matches a partition key → do NOT partition; use a plain index instead
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  AccessPattern ──→ PartitionChoiceService.choose()

  dominant filter?
    ├─ date range (txn_date)          → RANGE   (prunes to month, easy archive)
    ├─ few discrete values (region)   → LIST    (prunes to that value)
    ├─ high-card equality (account)   → HASH    (even spread, prunes to one)
    ├─ account equality + date window → COMPOSITE range(date)+hash(account)
    └─ none of the above              → NONE    (plain index, don't partition)

  PRUNING in action:
    WHERE txn_date in Feb AND account='SAV2001'
      │ prune by date  → transactions_2024_02
      │ prune by hash  → transactions_2024_02_h1   ← scans ONE sub-partition

  THE TRAP:
    partitioned by date, query WHERE account='SAV2001' (no date)
      │ cannot prune → scans Jan,Feb,Mar,... ALL partitions (slower than index)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Partitioning does not automatically make queries faster, and this is the single most misunderstood thing about it. Partitioning is primarily a manageability feature, and it only speeds up queries through partition pruning, which has a strict precondition: the query must filter on the partition key. Pruning is the planner eliminating partitions that cannot contain matching rows. If a table is partitioned by date into monthly partitions and I query a February date range, the planner proves only the February partition can match and scans just that one — that is where the speedup comes from.

The trap is querying by a column that is not the partition key. If the table is partitioned by date but my dominant query filters by account id with no date, the planner cannot know which months hold that account, so it cannot prune and must scan every partition. That is usually slower than an unpartitioned table with a good index, because instead of one index lookup I now do a lookup in every partition and combine the results. The row count never changed; I just scattered the data in a way that does not match how I query it.

So the scheme must come from the actual access pattern. Range partitioning fits a continuous ordered key queried by ranges, above all time, and it enables cheap archival by dropping old partitions. List partitioning fits a discrete key with a small set of known values, like region or account type. Hash partitioning fits a high-cardinality key with no natural ordering where I mainly do equality lookups, because it spreads data evenly and prunes to the single partition the hash lands in. When I query by two dimensions, such as per-account lookups and date windows, I use composite partitioning — range by date then sub-partition by hash of account — so both common filters can prune.

At the National Bank of India we partitioned transactions by month because the table was enormous, but our busiest query was all of a customer's transactions with no date filter, so the planner scanned every partition and performance actually got worse. I redesigned it as a composite scheme, range by date and sub-partitioned by hash of account, so a per-customer query within a date window prunes first to the month and then to one hash sub-partition. The rule I always state is that partitioning helps only when the query filters on the partition key, so I choose range, list, or hash to match how we actually query, and if nothing filters on a good key I do not partition at all and use a plain index instead.

---

keyPoints: Partitioning: split one table into segments (same DB)
Sharding: split data across multiple databases/servers
Range partitioning: by date. Hash partitioning: by key hash
Shard key choice is critical — bad key causes hot spots
